x: A zero-dependency React library for virtual-scrolling **waterfall (masonry)** and **equal-height** layouts, with infinite scroll and layout switching driven by your API. Features Virtual scrolling – only items near the viewport are rendered, so very long lists stay fast. Waterfall layout – Pinterest style, each item goes to the shortest column. Equal-height layout – Google Photos style, every row has the same height and each image keeps its aspect ratio. Dynamic layout – let the first API response decide which of the two layouts is used. Infinite scroll – built on IntersectionObserver with a configurable preload distance; only one page request is in flight at a time. Responsive – the container width is observed, columns and rows are recomputed when it changes. Written in TypeScript, with a peer dependency on React 16.8 or newer and no other dependencies. Installation Shell npm install react-hybrid-masonry # or yarn add react-hybrid-masonry # or pnpm add react-hybrid-masonry Quick start All three components share one contract: loadData(page, pageSize) returns { data, hasMore } , every item has a width and a height, and renderItem draws an item at the position the library computed. TSX import { VirtualMasonry } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; export function Gallery ( ) { const loadData = async ( page : number , pageSize : number ) => { const res = await fetch ( "/api/images?page=" + page + "&size=" + pageSize ) ; const json = await res . json ( ) ; return { data : json . items , hasMore : json . hasMore } ; } ; return ( < VirtualMasonry loadData = { loadData } pageSize = { 30 } minColumnWidth = { 200 } maxColumnWidth = { 350 } gap = { 16 } renderItem = { ( item ) => ( < div key = { item . id } style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height } } > < img src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" } } /> </ div > ) } /> ) ; } Which component should I use? Component Layout Use it for VirtualMasonry Waterfall: equal-width columns, items of different heights Image walls, product feeds, cards of different heights FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry Rows of equal height that fill the full width Photo albums, timelines, search results made of images DynamicMasonryView Either of the two, chosen at runtime When the back end or the content decides how a list is shown The data contract The components need the size of every item to compute its place before the image has loaded. The size is read from the first of these field pairs that exists: width / height , w / h , imgW / imgH . For any other shape pass mapSize : TSX < VirtualMasonry mapSize = { ( raw ) => ( { width : raw . cover . w , height : raw . cover . h } ) } /* ... */ / > Every item handed to renderItem is your original object plus the computed x , y , width and height (and widthRatio ). Your own fields such as url or title are preserved. The render contract The root element returned by renderItem must be absolutely positioned with the given left , top , width and height . Set a stable key (for example item.id ) on that element. In the waterfall layout the index argument counts only the items currently rendered and changes while scrolling. The components scroll with the window , not with an inner container. See the FAQ . Next: read the page for the component you picked, or jump to the pagination guide .

A Pinterest style waterfall layout: columns have the same width, items keep their aspect ratio and go into the shortest column. Only the items near the viewport are rendered. Overview VirtualMasonry arranges items in columns of equal width: every new item goes into the currently shortest column, and its height follows its own aspect ratio . The column count follows the container width (or you set it), so the same data is 2 columns on a phone and can be 6 on a wide screen. It suits image walls, product feeds and content cards of different heights. A 4-column layout with a 12px gap. The numbers show the order in which items were placed: each new item goes into the column that is shortest at that moment, so consecutive numbers are not necessarily in the same row. Columns have the same width and item heights follow the aspect ratio in your data, independent of the image download. Only items within buffer pixels of the viewport are rendered, so thousands of cards do not slow the page down. The next page is requested as the user nears the bottom, with a single request in flight at a time. Columns and positions are recalculated when the container width changes. Quick start TSX import { VirtualMasonry } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; type Pin = { id : number ; url : string ; title : string ; width : number ; height : number } ; async function loadData ( page : number , pageSize : number ) { const res = await fetch ( "/api/pins?page=" + page + "&size=" + pageSize ) ; const json = await res . json ( ) ; return { data : json . items as Pin [ ] , hasMore : json . hasMore as boolean } ; } export function PinBoard ( ) { return ( < VirtualMasonry loadData = { loadData } pageSize = { 30 } minColumnWidth = { 200 } maxColumnWidth = { 350 } gap = { 16 } renderItem = { ( item ) => ( < div key = { item . id } style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height } } > < img src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } loading = " lazy " style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" , display : "block" } } /> </ div > ) } /> ) ; } Every item needs a width and a height before it loads: the component computes positions from them. See data and sizes below. Data and sizes Where sizes come from The size of each item is read from the first pair of fields that exists: width / height , w / h , imgW / imgH . Use mapSize when your data is shaped differently: TSX < VirtualMasonry mapSize = { ( raw ) => ( { width : raw . cover . w , height : raw . cover . h } ) } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> The layout only uses the height / width ratio, so any unit works: pixels, or plain ratio values such as 4 and 3 . Items without valid sizes cannot be laid out: a missing width or height gives NaN , and the positions of every item after it break. If the API may omit fields, give mapSize a fallback, for example { width: raw.w || 4, height: raw.h || 3 } . What renderItem receives The item passed to renderItem(item, index) is your original object plus the fields below, calculated by the layout. Your own fields ( url , title , ...) are kept: Field Meaning x Distance from the left edge of the container (px). May be fractional. y Distance from the top of the container (px). May be fractional. width The column width (px), the same for every item in one layout. It replaces the width in your data . height The height calculated from the aspect ratio (px). It replaces the height in your data . widthRatio The original aspect ratio width / height . index is the position of the item among the currently rendered items . It changes while scrolling, so do not use it as a key . To keep the original dimensions, have your API use other field names such as w / h and read them through mapSize . Positions and sizes can be fractional; if you need whole pixels, round them yourself in renderItem . Rendering cards The root element you return must be absolutely positioned with the left , top , width and height you receive. Give the root element a stable key , such as item.id . Inside the card you are free to lay things out: image, title, buttons. The height is item.height , and the content has to fit it. For images use width: 100%; height: 100%; object-fit: cover , so they do not distort when the ratio differs from the data. TSX const Card = React . memo ( function Card ( { item } : { item : Pin & { x : number ; y : number ; width : number ; height : number } } ) { return ( < article style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height , overflow : "hidden" , borderRadius : 12 , } } > < img src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } loading = " lazy " style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" , display : "block" } } /> </ article > ) ; } ) ; < VirtualMasonry loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { ( item ) => < Card key = { item . id } item = { item } /> } /> While the width stays the same the layout result is stable, and visible items keep the same object reference as you scroll, so wrapping the card in React.memo avoids re-rendering it on scroll, see performance tuning . Props Prop Type Default Description loadData (page, pageSize) => Promise<{ data: any[]; hasMore: boolean }> – Load one page of data. Pages start at 1. Without it the component stays empty. renderItem (item, index) => ReactNode required Render one item. index is its position among the currently rendered items. pageSize number 50 Number of items requested per page. minColumnWidth number 200 Minimum column width (px), used to derive the column count. maxColumnWidth number – Maximum column width (px). columns number – Set the column count directly instead of deriving it from the width. gap number 16 Horizontal and vertical space between items (px). buffer number 1500 Extra distance above and below the viewport that is still rendered (px). loadMoreThreshold number 800 How far from the bottom (px) the next page is requested. mapSize (raw) => { width, height } – Map your data to a width and height. initialItems any[] – A first page you already have (for example prefetched during SSR). Page 1 is not requested again; loading continues from page 2. initialHasMore boolean true Used with initialItems : whether more data exists after the first page. enableAnimation boolean true Reserved, currently has no effect. Columns and column width The column count is determined in this order: If columns is set it is used as is, and the width options no longer take part. Otherwise start with floor(container width / minColumnWidth) columns, at least 1. If maxColumnWidth is set and the columns are wider than it, columns are added one by one (up to 20) until they fit; but if one more column would make them narrower than minColumnWidth , no further column is added. When the two limits cannot both be met, the minimum wins. The column width is (container width - gap * (columns - 1)) / columns , capped at maxColumnWidth . Here is what the same rules produce (16px gap): Container width minColumnWidth={200} minColumnWidth={200} maxColumnWidth={210} 320px 1 cols · 320px 1 cols · 210px (110px empty on the right) 480px 2 cols · 232px 2 cols · 210px (44px empty on the right) 768px 3 cols · 245px 3 cols · 210px (106px empty on the right) 1024px 5 cols · 192px 5 cols · 192px 1280px 6 cols · 200px 6 cols · 200px 1440px 7 cols · 192px 7 cols · 192px 1920px 9 cols · 199px 9 cols · 199px The minimum width does not include the gap : step 2 divides the container width by minColumnWidth without subtracting gap , so the real column width can be slightly below minColumnWidth (by less than one gap ). In the table, 1024px gives 5 columns of 192px while minColumnWidth is 200. When maxColumnWidth takes effect the grid is left-aligned and the right side stays empty, see the FAQ below. To hit the design's column count exactly at every width, use columns and pass it per breakpoint. Placement rules Each item goes int

x: A Google Photos style layout: images keep their aspect ratio, every row has the same height, and rows are scaled to fill the container width exactly. Only the rows near the viewport are rendered. Overview FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry lays images out row by row: every row has the same height and ends at the right edge, and every image keeps its own aspect ratio . How many images fit in a row follows from their proportions rather than from a fixed number of columns, which makes it a good fit for photo albums, timelines and search results where the images are the content. Layout for a 640px container with a 90px target row height and 6px gap (4 rows, the numbers are the image aspect ratios). Solid rows end at the right edge; the dashed last row keeps its natural proportions and is not stretched. All rows have the same height, and the gap between rows and between images is gap . Each image keeps its aspect ratio, with only a small deviation, see how the options work together . Only rows within buffer pixels of the viewport are rendered, so thousands of images do not slow the page down. The next page is requested as the user nears the bottom, with a single request in flight at a time. See data and sizes below. Data and sizes Where sizes come from The size of each item is read from the first pair of fields that exists: width / height , w / h , imgW / imgH . Use mapSize when your data is shaped differently: TSX < FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry mapSize = { ( raw ) => ( { width : raw . cover . w , height : raw . cover . h } ) } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> Internally the component turns width / height into a widthRatio per image, and the whole layout depends on that ratio only, so any unit works: pixels, or plain ratio values such as 4 and 3 . Items without valid sizes cannot be laid out: a missing width or height gives NaN and every position in that row breaks. If the API may omit fields, give mapSize a fallback, for example { width: raw.w || 4, height: raw.h || 3 } . What renderItem receives The item passed to renderItem(item, index) is your original object plus the fields below, calculated by the layout. Your own fields ( url , title , ...) are kept: Field Meaning x Distance from the left edge of the container (px). y Distance from the top of the container (px). width Laid-out width (px). It replaces the width in your data . height Laid-out height (px), the same for every image in a row. It also replaces the height in your data . widthRatio The aspect ratio width / height . index is the position of the item among all loaded data . It stays the same while scrolling, so it is safe to use for a key or for tracking. To keep the original dimensions, have your API use other field names such as w / h and read them through mapSize . Rendering cards The root element you return must be absolutely positioned with the left , top , width and height you receive. Give the root element a stable key , such as item.id . Use object-fit: cover on images. To make each row end exactly at the edge an image's ratio can deviate slightly, and cover turns that deviation into a sliver of cropping instead of distortion. Put captions on top of the image. The layout decides the row height, so there is no extra space below an image. Props Prop Type Default Description loadData (page, pageSize) => Promise<{ data: any[]; hasMore: boolean }> – Load one page of data. Pages start at 1. renderItem (item, index) => ReactNode required Render one positioned item. index is its position among all loaded data. pageSize number 50 Number of items requested per page. targetRowHeight number 245 Target row height; decides how many images go into a row. The actual height is adjusted within sizeRange . sizeRange [number, number] [230, 260] Allowed row height [min, max] . maxItemWidth number 975 Maximum width of a single item. maxStretchRatio number 1.5 A row keeps taking images until filling it needs an enlargement no greater than this value. Shrinking is not limited. gap number 8 Horizontal and vertical space between items (px). buffer number 1500 Extra distance above and below the viewport that is still rendered (px). loadMoreThreshold number 500 How far from the bottom (px) the next page is requested. mapSize (raw) => { width, height } – Map your data to a width and height. enableAnimation boolean true Reserved, currently has no effect. This component currently has no initialItems / initialHasMore ; the first page is loaded through loadData after mounting. When you need full control of the data, use the Core component below. How the options work together targetRowHeight and sizeRange The two options do different jobs. targetRowHeight decides how many images go into a row : the component uses it to compute each image's ideal width and keeps adding images until filling the row needs an enlargement no greater than maxStretchRatio . sizeRange decides the final row height limits : the height needed to fill the row is clamped into this range, and then the image widths are distributed proportionally so the row ends exactly at the container edge. Target row height 50px: 3 rows, more images per row. Target row height 100px: 5 rows, fewer images per row. To make images larger overall, raise targetRowHeight and sizeRange together. If you raise only one of them, the other pulls the row height back. maxStretchRatio It controls how much a row is willing to enlarge its images. A smaller value makes a row take more images before it ends, so images are enlarged less; a larger value ends rows earlier with fewer images that are enlarged more. Shrinking is not limited. maxStretchRatio 1.5: 4 rows. maxStretchRatio 1.2: 3 rows, denser rows overall. maxItemWidth The width limit of a single image. A very wide

h.t: Three ways to decide the layout

x: One component, two layouts. The layout is decided by a prop, by the first API response, or by a default. Overview DynamicMasonryView is a selector around VirtualMasonry (waterfall) and FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry (equal-height): the API tells it which presentation a list should use , so operations or the backend can switch per content (image-first or text cards) without the frontend maintaining two pages. How the layout is decided: the isMasonry prop first; if it is missing, page 1 is requested and its response is checked for isMasonry ; if that is missing too, defaultIsMasonry is used. The dashed path is a failed page 1 request. The component only selects. Layout, virtual scrolling and paging are done by the two inner components and behave exactly as they do on their own. Both layouts share one loadData , one renderItem and one mapSize , so you write a single data layer and a single card. In uncontrolled mode page 1 is requested only once: the request used to read the layout type is handed straight to the inner component. Quick start The most common use: the API tells the component which layout to use in the first page. TSX import { DynamicMasonryView } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; async function loadData ( page : number , pageSize : number ) { const res = await fetch ( "/api/content?page=" + page + "&size=" + pageSize ) ; const json = await res . json ( ) ; return page === 1 ? { data : json . items , hasMore : json . hasMore , isMasonry : json . layoutType === "waterfall" } : { data : json . items , hasMore : json . hasMore } ; } export function Feed ( ) { return ( < DynamicMasonryView loadData = { loadData } pageSize = { 30 } waterfallConfig = { { minColumnWidth : 200 , maxColumnWidth : 350 , gap : 16 } } equalHeightConfig = { { targetRowHeight : 245 , sizeRange : [ 230 , 260 ] , gap : 8 } } renderItem = { ( item , index , isMasonry ) => ( < div key = { item . id } style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height , borderRadius : isMasonry ? 12 : 6 , overflow : "hidden" , } } > < img src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" , display : "block" } } /> </ div > ) } /> ) ; } Every item needs a width and a height before it loads: both layouts compute positions from them. The contract is the same as for VirtualMasonry and FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry . Three ways to decide the layout 1. Controlled TSX < DynamicMasonryView isMasonry = { useWaterfall } // true = waterfall, false = equal-height loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { ( item , index , isMasonry ) => /* ... */ null } /> This prop has the highest priority. When it is passed, the component does not request page 1 up front to determine the layout, and any isMasonry in the loadData result is ignored. When it changes, the current layout component is unmounted, the other one is mounted, and the list loads from page 1 again. 2. From the first API response Without an isMasonry prop, the component calls loadData(1, pageSize) once after mounting, reads isMasonry from the result and caches that first page, so the chosen layout shows it immediately and page 1 is not requested a second time. The layout type is read only once ; later pages do not need to return it. 3. The default If loadData does not return isMasonry , defaultIsMasonry is used (default true , the waterfall). It is also used when no loadData is passed. If the first request fails, onError is called and the default layout is used. There is no cached page 1 then, so the inner component requests page 1 again; if that fails too, the inner component stops paging instead of retrying forever. Controlled switching example When the user chooses the presentation, keep the state yourself: TSX function Gallery ( ) { const [ isMasonry , setIsMasonry ] = useState ( true ) ; return ( < > < div role = " group " aria-label = " Layout " > < button aria-pressed = { isMasonry } onClick = { ( ) => setIsMasonry ( true ) } > Waterfall </ button > < button aria-pressed = { ! isMasonry } onClick = { ( ) => setIsMasonry ( false ) } > Equal height </ button > </ div > < DynamicMasonryView isMasonry = { isMasonry } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> </ > ) ; } Switching remounts the layout component and the list loads from page 1 again, and the scroll position is not kept, see the FAQ. onLayoutTypeLoaded is called on mount and every time isMasonry changes. Controlled mode has no "waiting for the layout type" phase, so renderInitialLoader is never shown. renderItem and cards renderItem(item, index, isMasonry) has one more argument than on the individual components: it tells you which layout this render is for, so one card can adapt to both. The fields of item ( x , y , width , height , ...) are the same as for the corresponding component, and the root element must be absolutely positioned as well. Waterfall ( isMasonry is true ) Equal height ( isMasonry is false ) index Position among the currently rendered items; changes while scrolling Position among all loaded data; stays the same while scrolling item.width The column width, the same for every item in one layout Different for every image item.height Calculated from the ratio, different per item The same within a row Card content Heights may differ, good for cards with text Image-first, text sits on top of the image In both layouts use a stable value such as key={item.id} ; do not use index as the key . Options for the two layouts waterfallConfig goes to the waterfall and equalHeightConfig to the equal-height layout. Fields you do not pass use the defaults of the corresponding component, and the two objects do not affect each other, so you can write both and let the API decide which one is used. waterfallConfig Field Type Default Description minColumnWidth number 200 Minimum column width (px), used to derive the column count. maxColumnWidth number – Maximum column width (px). columns number – Set the column count directly instead of deriving it from the width. gap number 16 Space between items (px). buffer number 1500 Extra distance above and below the viewport that is still rendered (px). The column count rules are in columns and column width of VirtualMasonry . equalHeightConfig Field Type Default Description targetRowHeight number 245 Target row height; decides how many images go into a row. sizeRange [number, number] [230, 260] Allowed row height range. maxItemWidth number 975 Maximum width of a single item. maxStretchRatio number 1.5 How much a row is willing to enlarge its images. gap number 8 Space between items (px). buffer number 1500 Extra distance around the viewport that is still rendered (px). How the fields work together is explained in the options of FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry . Keep sizeRange outside the component or in useMemo , so a new array on every render does not make every row recalculate. Only the fields above are exposed. loadMoreThreshold , initialItems and initialHasMore are not available through DynamicMasonryView ; the inner components use their own defaults (800 for the waterfall, 500 for the equal-height layout). Use the individual component directly when you need them. Props Prop Type Default Description isMasonry boolean – Controlled mode. true is the waterfall, false the equal-height layout. defaultIsMasonry boolean true Used when loadData does not return isMasonry (or no loadData is passed). loadData LoadDataFn – (page, pageSize) => Promise<{ data, hasMore, isMasonry? }> . renderItem (item, index, isMasonry) => ReactNode required Render function; the last argument says which layout is in use. waterfallConfig { minColumnWidth, maxColumnWidth, columns, gap, buffer } {} Passed to VirtualMasonry . equalHeightConfig { targetRowHeight, sizeRange, maxItemWidth, maxStretchRatio, gap, buffer } {} Passed to FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry . pageSize number 50 Number of items requested per page. mapSize (raw) => { width, height } – Map you

h.t: The life cycle of a page
Using React Query, SWR and similar

x: How pages are requested, when the next page starts, what happens on errors and how to start over. The loadData contract TSX type LoadData = ( page : number , // starts at 1 and increases by 1 for every successful request pageSize : number , ) => Promise < { data : any [ ] ; hasMore : boolean } > ; The component keeps all loaded items. loadData only returns the new page and the library appends it. The page number is kept internally, you do not have to count. Once hasMore is false no request is made any more. The life cycle of a page Stage When What happens First load When the component mounts Requests page 1 (not when initialItems is passed; the next request is then page 2). Trigger The trigger element at the bottom enters "viewport + loadMoreThreshold " Calls loadData(next page, pageSize) . In flight Between sending the request and its response No new request is started. Success loadData resolves The data is appended, the page number goes up, hasMore is updated, and the component immediately checks whether it should continue. Failure loadData rejects Logged with console.error , hasMore becomes false and automatic paging stops. Done hasMore is false The trigger is no longer observed and nothing is requested. When the next page starts A 1px marker sits at the bottom of the layout and an IntersectionObserver with a rootMargin of loadMoreThreshold watches it, so the next page is requested while the bottom is still loadMoreThreshold px away from the viewport. The dashed frame is the render range set by buffer , the blue solid frame is the viewport. When the trigger element (the thick line at the container bottom) enters "viewport plus loadMoreThreshold ", the next page is requested. After every page the observer subscribes again and immediately checks the current state: if the marker is still near the viewport (fast scrolling outran the content), the next page starts at once, so it never gets stuck because "no boundary was crossed". Choosing loadMoreThreshold and pageSize When users scroll fast or the API is slow, raise loadMoreThreshold so data arrives before the user reaches the bottom. The price is loading data the user may never scroll to. pageSize has to fill more than one screen. A rough way to estimate: the number of items that fit one screen is about "viewport height ÷ average item height × columns", and pageSize should be about twice that. With a page that is too small the trigger is still visible after every response, and requests are sent one after another. A page that is too large slows the first screen and every single request. Start at 30 to 50 and adjust to the real speed of your API. One request at a time While a request is in flight no new one is started. The check is synchronous, so several triggers within the same frame still send a single request, responses cannot arrive out of order, and page numbers always match the data. Because requests are sent strictly in page order, one at a time, you can safely use a cursor kept in a closure inside your loadData (see cursor pagination below) without handling concurrency. Showing an end-of-list message The component does not render anything at the end of the list. If you want a message, record hasMore in your own loadData and show it under the list: TSX function Board ( ) { const [ done , setDone ] = useState ( false ) ; const loadData = useCallback ( async ( page : number , pageSize : number ) => { const res = await fetchImages ( page , pageSize ) ; if ( ! res . hasMore ) setDone ( true ) ; return res ; } , [ ] ) ; return ( < > < VirtualMasonry loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> { done && < p style = { { textAlign : "center" } } > That is everything </ p > } </ > ) ; } When a request fails When loadData rejects, the error is logged with console.error and automatic paging stops ( hasMore becomes false ), so a broken API is not called in an endless loop while the marker is still visible. You can recover in the way that suits you: Remount the component with a new key to start again from page 1. Retry inside your own loadData : return normally once a retry succeeds; if every retry fails, throw the error so the component stops paging. Do not return { data: [], hasMore: true } after a failure to "keep paging": the component treats the page as successful and the page number goes up, so the failed page is skipped. To continue, retry the same page inside the function. Retrying with backoff TSX async function withRetry < T > ( fn : ( ) => Promise < T > , retries = 3 ) : Promise < T > { let lastError : unknown ; for ( let attempt = 0 ; attempt <= retries ; attempt ++ ) { try { return await fn ( ) ; } catch ( error ) { lastError = error ; await new Promise ( ( resolve ) => setTimeout ( resolve , 2 ** attempt * 500 ) ) ; // 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s } } throw lastError ; // still failing: hand it to the component, which stops paging } const loadData = ( page : number , size : number ) => withRetry ( ( ) => fetchImages ( page , size ) ) ; Cursor pagination The argument of loadData is a page number, but when your API uses a cursor , keep the cursor in a closure. h.t: What runs on the server and what in the browser
SEO: what is in the server HTML
Filters that come from the URL

x: What can run on the server, what has to wait for the browser, and how to hand over a prefetched first page. What runs on the server and what in the browser What Server Browser Measuring the container width Not executed Measured right after mounting Computing item positions Not executed (width unknown) Computed once the width is measured Rendering cards ( renderItem ) Not rendered , the output is an empty container Rendered Requesting the first page You fetch it on the server and pass initialItems Requested after mounting when there is no initialItems Scrolling, paging, IntersectionObserver Not executed Executed In one sentence: on the server the component outputs only an empty placeholder container and everything starts in the browser. That makes hydration safe by nature, at the price that the server HTML contains no cards. Add the use client directive The components use React hooks and are published without the directive. In the Next.js App Router, import them in a client file: TSX "use client" ; import { VirtualMasonry } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; export default function Gallery ( { first } : { first : { items : any [ ] ; hasMore : boolean } } ) { return ( < VirtualMasonry initialItems = { first . items } initialHasMore = { first . hasMore } loadData = { ( page , size ) => fetch ( "/api/images?page=" + page + "&size=" + size ) . then ( ( r ) => r . json ( ) ) } renderItem = { ( item ) => < Card item = { item } /> } /> ) ; } The Pages Router does not need the directive; import the components in a page or a component as usual. Passing a prefetched first page Fetch page 1 in a server component and pass it as initialItems . The component starts from that data, shows no loading state and does not request page 1 again; the first loadData call requests page 2. TSX // app/gallery/page.tsx (server component) import Gallery from "./Gallery" ; export default async function Page ( ) { const res = await fetch ( "https://api.example.com/images?page=1&size=30" , { next : { revalidate : 60 } , // cache the first page for 60 seconds } ) ; const first = await res . json ( ) ; return < Gallery first = { { items : first . items , hasMore : first . hasMore } } /> ; } initialItems is only available on VirtualMasonry . The first page of DynamicMasonryView and FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry is loaded on the client. When you want to prefetch and use the equal-height layout, the equal-height layout can currently only request its first page on the client. initialItems passed to a client component has to be serializable plain data (objects, arrays, strings, numbers), without functions or class instances. Every item needs a width and a height, see data and sizes . Hydration is safe The layout effects use useLayoutEffect in the browser and fall back to useEffect on the server automatically. During server rendering the container width is unknown, so the first render on both sides is an empty container and there is no hydration mismatch. Positions are computed right after mounting, as soon as the width is measured. Because cards are only rendered in the browser, using window , Math.random() and other values that only make sense on the client inside renderItem is safe and does not trigger hydration warnings. Using next/image The root element of a card is absolutely positioned anyway, so you can give next/image the fill prop: it fills the card, whose size the layout decides. Write sizes according to the column width, otherwise Next downloads the largest size: TSX import Image from "next/image" ; < VirtualMasonry columns = { 4 } gap = { 16 } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { ( item ) => ( < div key = { item . id } style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height , overflow : "hidden" , borderRadius : 12 } } > < Image src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } fill sizes = " (max-width: 640px) 50vw, (max-width: 1024px) 33vw, 25vw " style = { { objectFit : "cover" } } /> </ div > ) } /> The percentages in sizes should roughly match your column count: 4 columns is 25vw . Image hosts have to be configured in images.remotePatterns in next.config . SEO: what is in the server HTML Because positions depend on the measured width, the server HTML contains no cards even when you pass initialItems . If search engines have to see this content, there are a few approaches that can be combined: Give the content crawlable paginated URLs : for example /gallery?page=2 , render the plain list of that page on the server (links and text) and connect them with ordinary "next page" links. Give every detail page its own URL and put it in the sitemap. The list is only the way in; the detail pages are what gets indexed. Use a self-referencing canonical on every paginated URL : do not point page 2 and later at page 1, or the later pages are not indexed on their own. TSX // app/gallery/page.tsx: a list for crawlers next to the waterfall for users import Gallery from "./Gallery" ; // In Next.js 15 searchParams is a Promise; in 13 and 14 it is a plain object export default async function Page ( { searchParams } : { searchParams : Promise < { page ? : string } > } ) { const page = Number ( ( await searchParams ) . page ?? 1 ) ; const data = await fetchImages ( page , 30 ) ; return ( < > < Gallery first = { { items : data . items , hasMore : data . hasMore } } /> { /* Server-rendered and crawlable: a real, visible "browse all" entry that matches the waterfall */ } < nav aria-label = " Browse all images " > < ul > { data . items . map ( ( item : any ) => ( < li key = { item . id } > < a href = { "/gallery/" + item . id } > { item . title } </ a > </ li > ) ) } </ ul > { data . hasMore && < a href = { "/gallery?page=" + ( page + 1 ) } > Next page </ a > } </ nav > </ > ) ; } What crawlers see has to match what users see, and ideally it is visible and useful to users too (for example a "browse all" area in the footer). Do not use it to hide text users cannot see, or search engines may treat it as cloaking. Filters that come from the URL In the App Router, filters usually come from the URL. Pass the current query as the key of the client component and the list restarts from page 1 whenever the filters change: TSX "use client" ; import { useSearchParams } from "next/navigation" ; export default function Gallery ( ) { const params = useSearchParams ( ) ; const query = params . toString ( ) ; return ( < VirtualMasonry key = { query } loadData = { ( page , size ) => fetch ( "/api/images?" + query + "&page=" + page + "&size=" + size ) . then ( ( r ) => r . json ( ) ) } renderItem = { renderCard } /> ) ; } useSearchParams needs a Suspense boundary in statically rendered pages. Wrap only the small component that calls it, not the whole page, otherwise none of the page content is in the first response. Lazy loading The layout only makes sense in the browser, so it can be split out of the first-screen bundle: TSX "use client" ; import dynamic from "next/dynamic" ; const Gallery = dynamic ( ( ) => import ( "./Gallery" ) , { ssr : false } ) ; Only do this when you do not rely on initialItems to avoid a loading flash. From Next.js 15 on, ssr: false can only be written in a client component. Other frameworks Client-only projects such as Vite or Create React App : use it directly, there are no extra requirements. Astro : mount the React component that contains it with the client:only="react" directive. Remix and other SSR frameworks : the component only outputs an empty container on the server, so it can be rendered directly; if your cards use browser-only APIs, wrap the whole block so it renders only after mounting, to be safe. h.t: By container width instead of window width

x: The layout follows the container width. This page shows how to control it at each size. How the width is measured The width of the layout container ( 100% of the parent's width) is read at the moments below, and state is only updated when the width really changed: When Purpose On mount The first width, so the layout can be computed. ResizeObserver notification The container width changed (window resize, dragging a split, a sidebar opening). Window resize Fallback: normal resizing while the document stays visible. visibilitychange Fallback: the tab was resized in the background, read again the moment it is visible. So the parent must have a real width. A hidden parent ( display: none ) renders nothing until it is shown. The two fallbacks make sure the layout is still correct after a tab was resized while in the background. Waterfall: limits by width With minColumnWidth and maxColumnWidth the column count follows the width, see columns and column width . That is enough when you only need columns of a sensible size. Here is what minColumnWidth={160} and gap={12} produce at various widths: Container width Columns and column width 320px 2 cols · 154px 375px 2 cols · 182px 768px 4 cols · 183px 1024px 6 cols · 161px 1280px 8 cols · 150px 1600px 10 cols · 149px 1920px 12 cols · 149px Waterfall: columns per breakpoint When the design asks for an exact column count at specific widths, work it out yourself and pass columns . matchMedia is cheaper than listening to resize : it only updates when a breakpoint is crossed: TSX import { useEffect , useState } from "react" ; const QUERIES = [ [ "(min-width: 1600px)" , 6 ] , [ "(min-width: 1280px)" , 5 ] , [ "(min-width: 992px)" , 4 ] , [ "(min-width: 640px)" , 3 ] , ] as const ; function pick ( ) { const hit = QUERIES . find ( ( [ query ] ) => window . matchMedia ( query ) . matches ) ; return hit ? hit [ 1 ] : 2 ; } function useColumns ( ) { const [ columns , setColumns ] = useState ( 2 ) ; // the server and the first render use the smallest count useEffect ( ( ) => { const lists = QUERIES . map ( ( [ query ] ) => window . matchMedia ( query ) ) ; const update = ( ) => setColumns ( pick ( ) ) ; update ( ) ; lists . forEach ( ( list ) => list . addEventListener ( "change" , update ) ) ; return ( ) => lists . forEach ( ( list ) => list . removeEventListener ( "change" , update ) ) ; } , [ ] ) ; return columns ; } function Gallery ( ) { const columns = useColumns ( ) ; return < VirtualMasonry columns = { columns } gap = { 16 } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> ; } With DynamicMasonryView the same works through waterfallConfig={{ columns }} . By container width instead of window width Choosing columns from the window width is inaccurate in split or sidebar layouts: the window is wide but the gallery only gets a small part of it. Measure the gallery's own container instead: TSX function useContainerWidth < T extends HTMLElement > ( ) { const ref = useRef < T > ( null ) ; const [ width , setWidth ] = useState ( 0 ) ; useEffect ( ( ) => { const el = ref . current ; if ( ! el ) return ; const observer = new ResizeObserver ( ( ) => setWidth ( el . clientWidth ) ) ; observer . observe ( el ) ; setWidth ( el . clientWidth ) ; return ( ) => observer . disconnect ( ) ; } , [ ] ) ; return { ref , width } ; } function Board ( ) { const { ref , width } = useContainerWidth < HTMLDivElement > ( ) ; const columns = width >= 1200 ? 5 : width >= 900 ? 4 : width >= 600 ? 3 : 2 ; return ( < div ref = { ref } > { width > 0 && < VirtualMasonry columns = { columns } gap = { 16 } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> } </ div > ) ; } You do not need this hook when you only use minColumnWidth and maxColumnWidth : the component already calculates from the width of its own container. The hook only helps when you want to set columns exactly. Equal-height layout The equal-height layout has no column count: whenever the width changes every row is built again by the same rules, so the number of images per row changes on its own. To adjust the look per breakpoint pass different targetRowHeight and sizeRange values, for example a smaller row height on phones. Here is how many images the same 20 pictures put in each row at different widths (first 5 rows; with only 20 pictures the last row can be short on wide screens): Container width Default (row height 245, gap 8) Phone (row height 120, gap 4) 375px 1 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 768px 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 4 · 4 · 4 · 4 · 4 1280px 3 · 3 · 4 · 3 · 4 6 · 6 · 6 · 2 1920px 5 · 5 · 5 · 5 10 · 9 · 1 With the same row height a narrow screen fits only 1 to 2 images per row, so on phones you usually lower the row height to keep about 2 images per row. Once it becomes visible it is measured and laid out again. With tabs, it is safer to mount only the list of the current tab. A hidden list that stays mounted does not trigger loading (invisible elements never enter the viewport), but its loaded data and computed positions still use memory. Inside a dialog, scrolling the dialog does not drive the list: the component follows the window scroll and does not support scrolling inside the dialog's own scroll container. When a long list has to be shown in a dialog, use a full-page layout without an inner scroll area. Touch devices Touch screens have no hover. If titles and actions on a card only appear on hover, they can never be seen on touch devices. Keep them visible with a media query: TSX . card - caption { opacity : 0 ; transition : opacity 0 . 2s ; } . card : hover . card - caption { opacity : 1 ; } @ media ( hover : none ) { . card - caption { opacity : 1 ; } } What resizing costs Every width change recalculates the layout of all loaded items. With thousands of items that is cheap (see the numbers in performance tuning ), but do not change gap , columns or size options on every animation frame. While you drag the window the browser fires ResizeObserver quickly and the component updates frame by frame. FAQ The component is inside a dialog or a tab and is empty when it opens. A hidden parent (display: none) has a width of 0, and the component renders nothing: positions can only be computed once a real width has been measured. When the container becomes visible, ResizeObserver and visibilitychange trigger a new measurement, so it normally lays itself out as soon as it is shown; if your dialog animation keeps the width at 0, mounting the component after the animation starts works as well. Is the column count based on the window width or the container width? The container width. The component measures its own outer container, so next to a sidebar or inside a split layout the columns follow the width it really gets, not the whole window. It is only based on the window when you choose columns yourself from window.innerWidth. Images are too large or too small on phones. h.t: How many cards render at once

x: What the library already does for you, and what your own cards should check. What is already optimised Only elements inside the viewport plus buffer are mounted; the rest costs nothing in the DOM. The scroll position is updated at most once per animation frame ( requestAnimationFrame ). Item objects keep the same reference while scrolling and only change when the items or the container width change, so memoized children do not re-render on every scroll. The layout is cached with useMemo , so scrolling never recalculates positions. Scroll state lives inside the component, so your parent component does not re-render on every frame. While scrolling, the component calls renderItem again every frame (for the visible items only). So cards must be wrapped in React.memo : the library keeps the item references stable, and that is what lets memo actually work. Measure first, then adjust Before tuning, know the current state. The simplest metric is how many cards are in the DOM right now: put a marker on the card root and run this in the console: TSX // put data-card on the card root, then: document . querySelectorAll ( "[data-card]" ) . length To find out Use How many cards are rendered at once The one-line console snippet above, or the Elements panel Which components re-render while scrolling React DevTools Profiler with "record why each component rendered" on Whether scrolling drops frames and where the time goes The Performance panel of Chrome DevTools, record a scroll How many image requests are in flight The Network panel filtered by Img The overall score Lighthouse on a production build, once for desktop and once for mobile How many cards render at once The render range extends buffer above and below the viewport, so the number of elements that exist at once is roughly "(viewport height + 2 × buffer) ÷ height one element takes × elements per row". For a 900px tall viewport here are estimates (an order of magnitude only, the real figure depends on card height and columns): buffer Render band height Waterfall (6 columns, average height 300, gap 16) Equal height (row height 245, gap 8, about 3 per row) 500px 1900px about 36 cards about 23 images 1000px 2900px about 55 cards about 34 images 1500px 3900px about 74 cards about 46 images 3000px 6900px about 131 cards about 82 images The default buffer is 1500 : a few dozen cards exist at a time and fast scrolling shows almost no blank space. On weak machines or with heavy cards you can lower it to 500 to 1000 ; on pages with many heavy images, halving it often reduces the number of simultaneous image requests noticeably. buffer buffer (default 1500 ) is the distance above and below the viewport that always stays mounted. A larger value leaves less blank space during fast scrolling but mounts more cards and requests more images at once; a smaller value is cheaper, but you can see content load during fast scrolling. When tuning buffer and loadMoreThreshold , watch the number of image requests and your performance score together, and do not keep raising a value just because the screen looks better. loadMoreThreshold A larger loadMoreThreshold starts the next request earlier, which hides latency but loads data the user may never scroll to. Choose it by API latency and page size, see pagination and infinite scroll . What the layout calculation costs Whenever the list of items or the container width changes, the positions of all loaded items are recalculated once, and the cost grows in proportion to the number of items. Scrolling itself never triggers a recalculation. Below are timings of the layout algorithm alone in Node on a development machine (without React rendering, an order of magnitude only): Loaded items Waterfall Equal height 1,000 under 1 ms about 2 ms 10,000 about 1 ms about 7 ms 50,000 about 15 ms about 30 ms So the layout itself is negligible for every loaded page and every window drag; what is really expensive is rendering cards, which buffer and the complexity of your cards decide. Keep option references stable : sizeRange is a dependency of the layout calculation, and writing sizeRange={[230, 260]} inline in JSX makes a new array whenever the parent re-renders, so all rows are recalculated. Move it outside the component or use useMemo . mapSize is read through a ref, so passing an inline function does not trigger a new layout. The layout is computed from them before the images load, so nothing jumps when an image arrives. Add loading="lazy" and decoding="async" to images and use thumbnails close to the displayed size. Use object-fit: cover so images do not distort when rounding makes the sizes differ slightly. TSX < img src = { item . thumb } alt = { item . title } width = { item . width } height = { item . height } loading = " lazy " decoding = " async " style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" } } /> Request images at the displayed size Inside renderItem you have the displayed width of the card, and multiplied by the device pixel ratio it is the image width you should request. If your image service resizes by width, you do not have to download the same large image on every screen: TSX function thumbUrl ( url : string , cssWidth : number ) { const dpr = typeof window === "undefined" ? 1 : Math . min ( window . devicePixelRatio || 1 , 2 ) ; return url + "?w=" + Math . ceil ( cssWidth * dpr ) ; // replace with your image service's parameter } < img src = { thumbUrl ( item . url , item . width ) } alt = { item . title } loading = " lazy " decoding = " async " /> Cards Wrap the card in React.memo . h.t: 2. Compute and clamp the row height

x: A step-by-step description of the row filling algorithm with an example computed from real numbers, useful when tuning `maxStretchRatio` and `sizeRange`. Input Each item has an aspect ratio r = width / height . Computed at the target row height H , an item's ideal width is r * H . These are the symbols used: Symbol Meaning Matching option W Container width Measured automatically g Space between items gap H Target row height targetRowHeight [minH, maxH] Allowed row height range sizeRange maxStretch The largest enlargement a row accepts maxStretchRatio maxW Maximum width of one image maxItemWidth A complete example All numbers below are computed with the same rules as the component. Setup: container width W = 640 , gap g = 6 , target row height H = 90 , sizeRange = [80, 100] , maxStretchRatio = 1.5 . Images arrive in order with the aspect ratios 3:2, 2:3, 4:3, 1:1, 16:9, ... The whole layout (4 rows). The first row is taken apart step by step below. 1. Build a row greedily Start a row with the next image. Before adding another image, compute the scale needed to make the current row fill the container: Text scale = (W - (n - 1) * g) / sum(r_i * H) // n images in the row If scale <= maxStretchRatio the row is full enough and ends. Otherwise add the next image and check again. Adding an image always brings the scale closer to 1. If the row already needs to shrink ( scale < 1 ) it ends as well; shrinking is not limited. This is how the first row goes: Images added so far Row width Σ r·H Available width W - (n-1)·g Scale scale Decision 3:2 135 640 4.74 4.74 > 1.5: add another 3:2, 2:3 195 634 3.25 3.25 > 1.5: add another 3:2, 2:3, 4:3 315 628 1.99 1.99 > 1.5: add another 3:2, 2:3, 4:3, 1:1 405 622 1.54 1.54 > 1.5: add another 3:2, 2:3, 4:3, 1:1, 16:9 565 616 1.09 1.09 ≤ 1.5: end the row The first row takes 5 images . Because a single image almost always needs a very large enlargement to fill a row, this rule needs no special case to guarantee at least two images per row. 2. Compute and clamp the row height Text rowHeight = H * scale rowHeight = clamp(rowHeight, minHeight, maxHeight) // sizeRange First row: rowHeight = 90 × 1.09 ≈ 98.1 , which is within [80, 100] , so the row height is 98 . sizeRange is an independent visual density limit, so it always applies. When the clamp prevents an exact fill, the next step still makes the row end at the edge. 3. Distribute widths without accumulating error The ideal width of each image is r_i * rowHeight . To make the row end exactly at the container edge, the right edge of image i is computed from the cumulative share of the ideal widths and then rounded: Text available = W - (n - 1) * g rightEdge_i = (sum(ideal_0..i) / sum(ideal_all)) * available + i * g width_i = round(rightEdge_i - x_i) The result for the first row: Image Ideal width r·rowHeight Right edge Final width 3:2 147.2 147.2 147 2:3 65.4 218.6 66 4:3 130.8 355.4 130 1:1 98.1 459.6 99 16:9 174.4 640.0 174 The widths 147 + 66 + 130 + 99 + 174 plus 4 gaps add up to exactly the container width 640. Rounding errors do not accumulate and are not pushed onto the last image (which would make its proportions deviate visibly from the real picture). Finally every width is limited to maxItemWidth . Where the aspect ratio deviation comes from : once the row height is clamped to sizeRange , widths are still distributed to fill the row, so the displayed width of an image is r * the row height needed to fill , while the displayed height is the clamped row height. The deviation factor is "row height needed to fill ÷ clamped row height". In the example above both are equal, so there is no deviation; only clamped rows have one. The narrower sizeRange is, the more rows get clamped and the more visible the deviation is; object-fit: cover turns it into a little cropping. 4. The last row The row at the end of the loaded data is not stretched ; its height is limited to between sizeRange[0] and targetRowHeight . If its natural width would exceed the container, every image in the row is scaled down by the same factor: overflowScale = (W - total gaps) / total ideal width . When it does not exceed it, every image keeps its natural width and the right side stays empty. When the next page arrives, the former last row becomes an ordinary row and is recalculated. 5. Virtualization Every item gets x , y , width , height and originalIndex . Only items that intersect "the viewport plus buffer " are rendered, with originalIndex as the React key. The minHeight of the container is the bottom of the last row. The whole thing as pseudocode Text i = 0 y = 0 while i < items.length: row = [items[i]]; i += 1 # 1. build the row greedily while i < items.length: scale = (W - (len(row) - 1) * g) / sum(r * H for r in row) if scale <= maxStretch: break row.append(items[i]); i += 1 isLast = (i >= items.length) # 2. row height scale = (W - (len(row) - 1) * g) / sum(r * H for r in row) rowHeight = H * scale rowHeight = clamp(rowHeight, minH, isLast ? H : maxH) # 3. widths ideal = [r * rowHeight for r in row] if isLast: factor = min(1, (W - gaps) / sum(ideal)) widths = [min(round(w * factor), maxW) for w in ideal] else: widths = rightEdges_to_widths(ideal, W, g) # by cumulative share, no accumulated error widths = [min(w, maxW) for w in widths] place(row, widths, y, round(rowHeight)) y += round(rowHeight) + g Edge cases Case Result A very wide panorama It takes a row of its own, its width is cut to maxItemWidth , and the row may end up short on the right. Very few images, only 1 row That row is the last row: not stretched, and no taller than targetRowHeight . Container width is 0 (hidden) No layout, the output is empty; recalculated once it becomes visible. Items without width and height The aspect ratio is NaN and that row and everything after it is misplaced; give mapSize a fallback. A very small upper bound of sizeRange The row height is clamped while widths still fill the row, so the aspect ratio deviation grows. Appending new data Rows that are already complete do not change; only the former last row is recalculated. Complexity and stability The whole layout is one front-to-back pass in which every item is visited a constant number of times, so the cost is proportional to the number of items. Laying out 10,000 images takes milliseconds, see performance tuning . The layout is deterministic : the same data, width and options always give the same result, so content does not jump while scrolling. Rows are built in order and the result of a row depends only on the rows before it and its own data, which is why appending data does not affect rows that are already complete. Tuning tips Many rows with only 2 images mean targetRowHeight is too large for the container width: lower it, or relax sizeRange . A very narrow sizeRange gives very even row heights but a larger aspect ratio deviation; relax it if you want more natural proportions. Lowering maxStretchRatio reduces enlargement, raising it makes rows end earlier. When you doubt the effect of a setting, work one row out by hand with the formulas above and compare it with the page. FAQ Why not use a globally optimal partitioning algorithm? Some libraries use linear partitioning (dynamic programming) to find one optimal split of all images into rows. The drawback is that appending data changes rows that were already laid out, so content jumps while scrolling. The greedy algorithm used here builds rows one by one in order: appending data only affects the last row, content you have already seen never moves, and the work is proportional to the number of images, which suits infinite scrolling. Why does a row contain only one image? That image is very wide (a panorama, for example), and on its own filling the row already needs an enlargement no greater than maxStretchRatio, so the row ends there. Its width is also capped at maxItemWidth; when that cap is below the container width the row ends up short on the right. Why are some rows slightly taller or shorter than

Common questions and the usual cause of problems. Does it scroll inside its own container? No. It follows the window scroll and reads its own position with getBoundingClientRect, so put it in a normally scrolling page. Scrolling inside a nested overflow container is not supported. Items are stacked at the top-left or overlap each other. Why? The root element returned by renderItem must use position: absolute together with the given left, top, width and height. Without it the browser lays the items out as normal blocks. The container is tall but empty. Positions are only computed after the container width has been measured, so a container that is hidden (display: none) or has zero width renders nothing. Make sure it has a real width. Opening a hidden tab triggers a re-measure through visibilitychange and ResizeObserver. Why do I get duplicate key warnings or flickering cards in the waterfall layout? In VirtualMasonry the second argument of renderItem is the index among the currently rendered items, not the index in your data, and it changes while you scroll. Always put a stable key (for example key={item.id}) on the element you return. Loading stopped and never continues. Either loadData returned hasMore: false, or a page request rejected. A failed request sets hasMore to false so the library does not retry in a loop. Remount the component (change its key) to start again, or retry inside loadData and return normally once a retry succeeds, throwing only if every retry fails. Do not return an empty page with hasMore: true: the page number advances and the failed page is skipped. The same page is requested twice. Only one request is in flight at a time, so this is almost always React StrictMode running effects twice in development, or the component being mounted twice. In DynamicMasonryView the page-1 response used to pick the layout is cached and reused, so page 1 is not requested again by the inner layout. The layout does not switch when I change the API response. In uncontrolled mode the layout type is read once, from the first loadData call. Pass the isMasonry prop to switch at runtime. Switching remounts the active layout and loads from page 1 again. I get a hooks error in the Next.js App Router. The components use React hooks and are not marked with the use client directive. Import them from a file that starts with use client. Does enableAnimation do anything? Not at the moment. It is accepted for API symmetry between the components and reserved for later; items are positioned without a transition. Which fields are used as the item size? width/height, then w/h, then imgW/imgH. Use mapSize for any other field names. Items without a valid size cannot be laid out, so make sure every item has one.

Notable changes to the library. 1.1.0 Added VirtualMasonry : columns to fix the column count, initialItems and initialHasMore to start from a prefetched first page. DynamicMasonryView : waterfallConfig.columns . Server rendering support: layout effects fall back to useEffect on the server. Changed Equal-height layout: new row building rule driven by maxStretchRatio , widths distributed from cumulative ratios so rounding errors no longer end up on the last image, and the last row is scaled down uniformly when it overflows. Waterfall layout: when maxColumnWidth is set, columns are only added while the new column width stays at or above minColumnWidth . Fixed Quick scrolling could start two page requests at once; a synchronous guard now allows a single request. A failed request is no longer retried in an endless loop; paging stops until the component is remounted. Container width could stay stale after a window was resized in a background tab; resize and visibilitychange now re-measure it. Equal-height scroll position used a cached offsetTop ; it now reads getBoundingClientRect , so content above the list can change height safely. Visible items kept a stable identity while scrolling, so memoized cards no longer re-render on every scroll event. 1.0.1 First public release on npm : VirtualMasonry , FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry and DynamicMasonryView .
